analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income paid by high earners.
analysis.headline: A Senate Republican bill to erase the new 3.8% tax on high earners' investment income was referred to the Finance Committee on August 5, 2010, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2010 health care law created a 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income — stock gains, dividends, interest, and rental and business profits — for individuals earning over $200,000 and couples over $250,000, starting in 2013. This bill would repeal that tax entirely. Repeal would cut taxes for the small share of households with substantial investment income and remove a dedicated funding stream for Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the tax cut would go almost entirely to households at the top of the income distribution — the roughly 2-3% of filers earning above $200,000 single / $250,000 joint who have enough investment income to owe the tax. That includes high earners with capital gains, dividends, interest, passive rental income, and profits passed through from businesses they own but don't actively run.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners with large investment income

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 1402 of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, erasing the 3.8% tax on net investment income before it ever took effect in 2013 [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purposes are to rescind the tax on investment income and to 'promote job creation and small businesses' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund would lose a dedicated funding stream, since the tax was added to shore up Medicare financing as part of the same 2010 law. The gains would flow to the top few percent of households, while the cost of that lost revenue would eventually be borne by anyone who relies on Medicare or by taxpayers generally through higher deficits or other taxes.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes a dedicated revenue source for Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund; the tax was enacted in the same 2010 reconciliation law specifically to extend that fund's solvency [S2].

The tax applies only to households earning over $200,000 ($250,000 for joint filers), so the benefit of repeal is concentrated among the highest-income investors rather than spread across working people [S2].

Supporters' own stated rationale — that the tax would hurt job creation and small business — depends on the claim that taxes on passive investment income flow through to hiring; the bill text offers no offsetting spending cuts or revenue replacements to cover the lost Medicare funding [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is a tax cut that lands almost entirely on the top few percent of households, and its cost is a dedicated Medicare funding stream that the 2010 law created to keep the hospital insurance trust fund solvent. The revenue side is concrete and immediate; the claimed job-creation benefit is a general assertion the bill does not document. On balance, the measure transfers resources upward while reducing health-insurance financing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on August 5, 2010, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. John Cornyn introduced the bill with Sens. Mike Crapo and Pat Roberts as original cosponsors on August 5, 2010 [S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 3.8% investment-income tax took effect in 2013 as scheduled, preserving Medicare funding while leaving the tax burden on high earners with investment income intact. Top-income investors, who would have received the tax cut, were the losers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare funding; high earners kept the tax

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 3.8% net investment income tax and delivered introductory remarks

for.name: Sens. Mike Crapo and Pat Roberts

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it remained pending in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Senate Republicans (3 of 40), and no Democrat cosponsored; the bill was one of many Republican repeal efforts following the 2010 health care law [S3][S4].

industries.industry: High-income investors (households earning over $200k/$250k with capital gains, dividends, interest, and passive income)
industries.note: Had the bill passed, these households would have avoided the 3.8% tax on their investment income; because the bill died, the tax took effect in 2013. Their interest runs against ordinary people here: the cut's funding stream was Medicare revenue.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through and passive businesses
industries.note: The bill's stated goal was to relieve small business and job creators, since passive business profits count as net investment income under the tax; repeal would have cut their bills. The tax stayed in place.
The dedicated 3.8% investment-income revenue stream was preserved when the bill died, supporting the hospital insurance trust fund that pays for seniors' hospital care.
